blocks.content: docker pull downloads an image from a registry to your local machine, but it is smarter than a plain file download, it only fetches the layers you do not already have.
docker pull takes a repository name and, optionally, a tag, and fetches that exact image from the configured registry, Docker Hub by default unless you specify another registry's hostname.

blocks.alt: Pull fetches the image and stores it locally

blocks.content:
docker pull nginx:1.25
docker pull myregistry.com/team/myapp:2.0

code.content:

docker pull myregistry.com/team/myapp:2.0

codes.bash:
docker pull nginx:1.25

blocks.content: Before downloading anything, Docker checks each layer the target image is made of against what you already have locally. If your machine already has a layer (from a previous pull of a related image, for example), that layer is skipped entirely, only genuinely new layers are transferred.

blocks.alt: Each layer is checked individually, not the image as one blob

blocks.content: If you omit a tag entirely, docker pull nginx is shorthand for docker pull nginx:latest. This is convenient for quick experiments, but risky for anything meant to be reproducible, since latest is just a label, not a guarantee of what version you will actually get on any given day.
4. A Pull Downloads Layer by Layer
blocks.text: 4. A Pull Downloads Layer by Layer

blocks.content: Watching a pull happen shows this layer-by-layer behavior directly, some lines finish almost instantly because Docker recognized it already had that layer cached, while genuinely new layers show real download progress.

blocks.alt: One pull can be a mix of cached and freshly fetched layers

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A pull is layer-aware, not a single monolithic download, only layers missing locally actually transfer over the network.
Always pin an explicit tag in anything meant to be reproducible, an untagged pull silently resolves to "latest".
